blocks.x: Okay. Reel number two at Tex Stevens, August the 29th, 1995. We're still at Tulane. So you're continuing that story on you. You got the fish in your… Yeah. And you were going to the hospital and you met your brother-in-law.

Right. Ivan Caldwell is his name, the late Ivan Caldwell. He was married to my sister-in-law, Rita. Well, incidentally, while I was in the hospital, I'm two degrees, I think, from death, so the doctor said. And I was just about going out of my head. Well, as I was slowly getting a little better, I had a lot of girlfriends come into the hospital to check me out because I was a single guy back in 1954. All right. So my current wife, who was Ivan Caldwell's sister-in-law at the time, she came up and I checked her out. Right. Well, of course. Well, you know how we say… What else?
You were a deaf store.

Right, right. But prior to that, I was sweet on her sister. I saw her sister who was already married and had three children, but I didn't know it at the time. So Ivan told me, he said, look, man, I can do you any good. Say, look, that sister-in-law, she's probably got three children already and another one might be on the way. He said, but the other sister, the other one you were checking out, she's single. That's the baby girl. I said, she seemed to not like me. I said, but I tell you what, I'm going to see if I can date her. Well, the whole while I was in the hospital, she really didn't like me. And so Ivan and I made a bet, I said, I tell you what I bet you. When I get out this daggone hospital and I show her that new automobile I have and I put on these pretty clothes when I go up to her. Well, I had already met her mother, so meeting her mother, that was a duel. Well, I went up there to the house after I got out of the hospital and I started talking to her mother. She was sitting outside in the swing. I said, hello, how are you? I said, I came by to see your mother and say hello and walked over her. And I guess she said it up by, damn, he's ignoring me. Well, somehow or another, I got back outside and I started talking. She was sitting in the swing with another young man who's a minister. Well, he wasn't a minister then, but I thought probably was her boyfriend. I didn't know, but it didn't matter to me one way or the other. I just came up to say hello to her mother and to let my brother-in-law know that I could date her and take her out. Well, it was about, it took me about, I'd say about three weeks to a month, but I finally got to her. She finally decided to go out with me and make a long story short, 1955 we got married. What is this? What's the date?
What's the date?

October the 8th, 1955. Yeah, I like that. That's my material. I got one for you too, Ted. This was the, you were on the Strong Stamp. Oh, okay. Just keep that, we'll get into that later. We'll get to the stamp.
Yeah. Okay, so you all finally got married and?
We finally got married and that's the story. Which church?
We got married up here at St.

What's this Catholic Church up here? I forgot, St. Joan of Arc. St. Joan of Arc. St. Joan of Arc. Even though I'm a Baptist, but I married Catholic because she went, that was it. That was it. But if you're a Christian and you have faith in people, you know, look, I like all people, all denominations. There's only one God anyway. And after all, all of us came through the same system that life was given to us through Almighty God and Jesus Christ and that's the way we're probably going to travel from this earth just like Adam and Eve did, wild into the ground or into a vault someplace.
So, okay, you know, that, that, so you, you seem like you were married later than, later than I thought. No.
From 55 until, until 95. How many years is that? Well, no, no, no.
I'm saying I thought you got, I thought you got married closer to after the war was over.
No. No, no, no, no, no, no.
Well, getting back, I had another question about the Sentinel. You, you talked about, about John Russo. Was, was Russo the editor?

John Russo was the editor at that time. And they had other people in there working under John Russo. I'm trying to think of a young man, well, an old guy, I can't think of his name right now. But he worked there as the assistant editor. He was a very nice man. He's, he's, he's dead now. And, they had a guy by the name of A.C. Jack Moore who contributed sports stories to the Louisiana Weekly. He's going on to his reward also. And, but there was some very nice people in the Informa Sentinel, like I said. It was, it was a challenge to Louisiana Weekly because it was an out of town paper. And, you know, anytime somebody from out of town, you always take a second look and say, well, what are they bringing in here? What are they doing that I'm not doing? And everybody looks at that, at competition, even in business today. People selling automobiles or what have you.
Well, when that was, how was, how was the Weekly, the Sentinel, and the Pittsburgh Courier, how was, how were those, how was that competition done?
Well, the competition.
What kind of market share did each one have?

Well, well, the, the Louisiana Weekly had the lion's share of paid circulation and readership. And the Pittsburgh Courier was second. The Informa Sentinel was like a Johnny come lately because a lot of people probably didn't know about it because, well, you wasn't getting any radio, well, you didn't have any television at that time of note. And all you could do, like I said, New Orleans didn't have shopping centers as we know them today. New Orleans was a little smaller city. But people got around to the Informa Sentinel eventually, but we never did top the sales posture of the Pittsburgh Courier or of the Louisiana Weekend. See, at that time, the Pittsburgh Courier, they had the manpower and they had the money. And they were really pressing the Louisiana Weekly. But the Informa Sentinel did not have the money like the Courier and the Weekly at that time. So all in all. What kind of circulation for the Sentinel?
Well, at that time. What was it supposed to be a week?

Well, let me start with the Louisiana Weekly. You've got to remember, Louisiana Weekly was going statewide. And especially in little country towns where they had never seen a black newspaper, let's say like former Louisiana, let's say like the southern part of Baton Rouge or just any particular outlying area away from any major metropolitan area. Louisiana Weekly was reaching, I would say, around about 30 or 40 little communities in and around the New Orleans area like Blackmon Parish, St. Bernard, and so forth and so on. Whereas the Pittsburgh Courier wasn't reaching that. The Pittsburgh Courier was concentrating on major metropolitan areas. Occasionally, if somebody would get off for train and take that paper to a little country town, they would say, I would like to see it because it was a very good publication. Well, the Informa Sentinel did not have, like I said, now outside of Houston, Texas, in and around the various counties outside. They knew about the Informa Sentinel, but the Informa wanted to broaden out into major areas. See, the Informa got into Baton Rouge, then they got into New Orleans, and now they got into other areas, but I wasn't concentrating on what was happening other than New Orleans.
Like the Pittsburgh Courier had a Louisiana edition. Did the Sentinel have a Louisiana edition separate, or was it all the same? No.
They had one special edition. They had one special edition. One special edition. Yeah. Enough of that.
I think I've got enough of that. On that, how did you, from the Sentinel, where did you work?

Well, from the Sentinel, what I did, like I told you, radio was coming in, in the focus at the time. And I ran into a young man by the name of Richard Rising, who was a white guy who was working at WJBW, radio station here on the corner of Camp and Canal. Well, I used to listen to Richard quite often. And, well, after about, maybe about a year or so, Richard and I developed a friendship over the telephone. So he asked me, said, why don't you come down and see what I'm doing one night? And I just got in my automobile or bus or whatever, and I went on down there and I sat in the studio with him and I watched what he was doing, you know? And Richard and I got to be very good friends. So after several months, I was saying to Richard, I said, hell, I'd like to do that one day. So Richard said, yeah, you would like to do it one day? I said, why don't you give it a try? I said, how? I said, nobody's going to hire me. Look at this paint job I have. So he said, why don't you come in and talk to Mrs. Colson? The Colson family was the ones who owned the WJBW at the time. So I put one of my best suits on and I went down there all polished and looking good and everything. And she said, well, we would love to have you, our techs. He said, but you can't do a broadcast from our station. I said, I can't. She said, no, but if you can find a facility where you can do a remote, we'd be glad to have you. Now, prior to this now, well, Richard decided to do a remote because he took a liking to me. The first place we did a remote was from the Gladstone Hotel on Dryad Street. This was before Daddy-O. See, Daddy-O was the first full-time disc jockey, but I was the first part-time disc jockey. I was on there before Daddy-O and before Anya Whip. So anyway, what really happened was that I would sit in with Richard as long as he was at the Gladstone Hotel. So eventually, what I did, I started selling the time for myself. I became my own broker, and I went to Butler Service Station. I went to this lounge or that lounge. I went to the Dewdrip. I went to whatever place. Then I went to, I think it was one of the drugstores in China, the Bell Fuels Drugstore, whatever. So I had about eight or ten clients where I could make myself some money. So I said, hell, this is going to be all right. So I started as a jazz disc jockey, and I moved from the Gladstone Hotel because what really happened, the kids from up here at Lowell and Tulane had picked up the radio station. WJBW were already listening to it anyway. And they said, hey, this guy is playing jazz down there. I said, well, come on down. And I used to say in the cool of the evening when you get ready to dish out that good old underprunder, Mr. Cool's going to be around. Doubting the ground and get from around to keep your boys. Don't make too much noise. Just hang with the boys. If you want to twirl and live in the world, you've got to hang with the girls. In order to get some money, you've got to have that money. So remember, reach for the sky. And remember, don't be shy. Just be cool, baby, and let it all hang out. That's the way I used to talk on radio.
Now, with the white kids from Tulane and Lowell, would they come down to the blinds, though?
That was the bulk of my artists. That was the bulk of my audience. It was mostly whites.
But you had mostly, you went to black advertising.
Well, I had to at that time.
Interesting. If you're going to whites.

Well, now, let me see. I did have some white advertising. I'm trying to think what white advertising is. The first white advertising I had was a grocery store down on, but it was a black guy that was running. It was a white, it was down on Caffin Avenue. I'm trying to think of the name of the store right now. It just escapes me. But it was a store run by black, but it was owned by white.
It's interesting that the woman who owned JBW would hire you to do a remote, but wouldn't let you be in the studio. But it was okay if you were someplace else.

Well, that was the law at the time, because, you know, the Carlson family were very beautiful people. I have great love for her son. I think his name was Richard Carlson, if you remember. Not Richard, it was something else. But anyhow, I know the last name was the Carlson family. They were very, she was a nice-looking lady, very cultured and polished and very businesslike. Well, that's the way I approached her, and that's the way she dealt with me. But you've got to remember, we're dealing with 1948, 49, and 50, and things were still segregated. Like I said, no shopping centers of note that we have today. And you've got to remember, you had the White Citizen Council, you had the Ku Klux Klan, and these people on the march, and right then and there, they're ready to talk that nigger would any time they felt like it, you know? Sure. I don't care what college you went to, or how smart you were, or how many degrees you had, you were still a nigger to a certain element of white people at that particular time. And here's a black guy saying nigger again, right? But after all, that's part of the American language, you know?
Getting back to, I'm saying laws and things, but you had white kids coming down to this black lounge. Black, right, right. And listening to, were there any problems there? No problem.

Mr. Hayes would not have anything like that. Mr. Hayes was the owner of Hayes' chicken shack. Oh, boy. Mr. Hayes was the owner of the house. He was a damn good business man, and he made sure that anybody who came in, you had to have collar and tie and a jacket on. You didn't come in there with no T-shirt on. That's right, white or black.
We were talking, but your remote was from the Gladstone.

From the Gladstone, and also from Hayes. Yeah, well, you see, the Gladstone started getting small, because when people found out that I was on the air, it started flooding the place. There was no place to put them, so I had to find another venue. So I had to go to Hayes, which was a larger place at the time. I should have brought the pictures and everything with me.
Now, Hayes was on Louisiana Avenue?
It was 20, 26, 21, Louisiana Avenue.
Not far from Flint Goodwitch?
Right down the street, two blocks from Flint Goodwitch's Hospital. Okay. Mm-hmm.
Yeah. But my point was, was there any problem with the whites coming into a black establishment? No problem.

No problem. No problems at all. We'll see, Mr. Hayes, I think, at that time, was contributing to whatever quality of life that we had at that time. He had good connections with the mayor at that time. I think it was Ski Row was the mayor at that time. And prior to Ski Row, you had a... Morrison.
Mayor Morrison.

Mayor Morrison. It could have been Morrison, I think. It was Morrison. Mayor Morrison. And so they, the laws made no trouble for Mr. Hayes. He made sure that they wouldn't make any trouble because he kept a very unique place, very likable place. People seemed to enjoy themselves when they came here. You had to come in there well, well-groomed, and your mannerism had to be at the highest level in order to get service. He made sure that everything was above board.
Was that, would you say, that that was true of most establishments, black establishments in the city?

No, well, you were a little more relaxed than some of the other clubs. If you went down to Albert Ellis' Horseshoe Lounge, you could be well-dressed, but you could go without a collar or a tie. You just show up and you could be there, and if you would go to Booker T. Washington, maybe you would probably, at that time, you would probably dress a little more because we were proud to have Booker T. Washington Auditorium because it was a new facility, and it was a little better than the Rosenwald thing down the street, which was in the same neighborhood with just around five or six blocks down the street from Booker T. Washington Auditorium. But it was a very nice place to enjoy yourself. Or either when you went to Club Desire or one of the clubs like that, you could either Club Rocket or Gypsy T. Rump, most of the time the blacks would dress accordingly, especially when you had the big bands coming in like Joe Liggins, or you had anybody coming in like some of the big-time bands like maybe Erskine Hawkins, maybe Bo Moose Jackson or Billie Holiday or some of the other talent because you wanted to be associated with that kind of talent, you see? And that was the days before rap became on the scene. Today you can wear anything, you go to a rap concert. You can go half nude even with your belly sticking out. Or even they got like the new pants I saw on television with all your behinds sticking out right now under plastic. How do you like that? Plastic pants. Plastic pants. How about that?
Yeah. Yeah. It's a new day. It's a new day. Okay, where were we? Okay, so after, I mean after the Sentinel, where, what other, did you work for another paper after that?

No, I did not. What I did, I stayed in radio until 1962. And I got a call from a friend of mine by the name of Dorsey who was working for the Urban League at that time. Ebony Magazine had a position open, and for some reason Dorsey picked me over whomever at the time. And to make a long story short, I came back and I talked to my wife. And my wife said, well, find out what they're paying and so forth and so on. And after all, we're gonna have a family and we need a little extra money. So I said, well, I can keep this and do this on the weekend. And I still work for Ebony Magazine. So I told Dorsey, okay. Well, what Dorsey did, Dorsey called New York. And Ben Wright, who was my immediate supervisor at the time, he called me long distance. I didn't know who he was. I said, hello? He said, I'm Ben Wright. I said, glad to know you. I said, where are you calling from? He said, I'm calling from New York. He said, I understand you're supposed to be coming to work for us. I said, who are you? He said, I'm Ben Wright. I'm with Ebony Magazine. I said, well, you didn't say that at first. Well, we had a conversation going, all right. So eventually, he said, well, look, Tex, I'm gonna send you plane fare and money's to travel to New York. So they sent me a package, nice package. Come to New York. I told my wife, I said, I'm going to New York. I'm gonna check them out. So Ebony put me to work with McCann, Erickson, and a couple of these other white firms to see if I had the background to work with them. Because they were already handling business for these major corporations. So I worked with them on certain assignments to do market research. I did all right. I won the Wright Fowler Award back then in 1962. I was so good, I felt proud of myself.
Oh, bitch.

So what was that award? Explain that award. That was an award for promotion. In other words, when you would call on somebody like Macy's, or you'd call on the Falstead Brewing Company, and if, in other words, they would, what you call, they would monitor you. And then the boss would call and say, how did my new representative appear to you? Did you like his professional approach and this, that, and the other? Yeah. So everywhere I went, I got less than 95. On 20 major calls in and around New York, everything I got was 95 to 100. I said I like his demeanor. I like his presentation. I like his style. I like his vocal rhythm, or whatever they were saying about me. Yeah. You know, it made me feel very good. I said, hell, you mean to tell me I'm big time in New York? How about that?
Yeah, a little guy from New Orleans makes it.

Little guy from New Orleans. Makes it. Now, I had my enemies up there. They had some blacks that was in New York. They just didn't like the idea of a southerner coming up there, taking a job with a position that I had. And see, after working there for around about five or six years, Mr. Johnson had offered me a vice presidency. But I couldn't take it because my children were growing up at the time. But see, what Mr. Johnson wanted me to do, he wanted me to sell my house and move to New York with my children. They were not used to living in 18, 20, and 30, and 40-story buildings, you know? I wasn't even in for that myself. And I just didn't want to give up my house. I could have been big time with Johnson, but Johnson didn't want to sign a contract with me. And so, well, here's what happened, see.
There's no guarantees.

There was no guarantee. Because already, I had been told by one or two other vice presidents, say, you've got to be careful now if you're coming up as a vice president. I said, Johnson, no sign any papers. He'd give you his word. He said his word is his bond, and most times he'd stick by it. I said, but I can't stand by no word, not when I have to pay bills, you know? I said, because Mad Dick comes with everybody, even after 40 years with the same woman. I'm still having arguments and fusses every now and then, some kind of fuss.
You know, I went ahead of myself, ahead of myself, because we were in radio, and I wanted to keep on that train.
You wanted to get into television?
No, no, no. That's a faster train. Let's go back. Let's go back for a second. So you worked at JBW. No. JBW, no. What was your further first station you went?

Well, after that, now, here comes WMRY, which is now WYLD. That's wild. WMRY started in the French Quarter by the Court of Two Sisters. Ernie Branger, who was Ernie the whip, he was the major black disc jockey down there. Well, Ernie and I had kept a beautiful relationship all of our lives because he knew my children, I knew his children, I knew his wife and so forth. Even his oldest child today still calls me his uncle. Well, anyway, Ernie and I were in high school together. So, Ernie said, why don't you come to work down here with us? Well, now, in the meantime, by working for myself, there was a gentleman by the name of, I'm trying to think of his name, an agency here by the name of Care Incorporated. So, he picked up whatever monies that I was making on my own and started paying me a salary to go to WMRY to work. That meant I didn't have to do any selling. They were gonna get the business for me. So, I said, well, it's all right by me. And that made me big time. And I started making more money. Eventually, the station took a liking to me because they were getting ready to move. Excuse me, we're knocking up the... So, they were getting ready to move. And they wanted me to come to work for them full time. And they made me another higher financial offer. So, I took that and I told Care goodbye, just like that. So, I wrote the contract with them. And I started working full time for WMRY. And those were the very beautiful days because I got more popular. People would come to the studio to see who I was. And remember, that was the first black radio station in the city. And a lot of people hadn't seen Ernie Branger, Ernie the Whip, myself, Malcolm Brown. Myself, Malcolm Plath, Bob Parker, Judge Israel Augustine.
Is Israel Augustine the same? He was a DJ?
He was a DJ. He worked part time in the evening. In fact, I'm the one who set up the Sundown Supper Club for him to work. How'd you like that?
What was the Sundown Supper Club?

That was a slow type combination jazz, pop type of program. Like, Body and Soul, This Love of Mine, Over the Rainbow. Ballad. Ballad kind of thing. But in other words, easy listening music with jazz overtones. That's what it was all about.
So, I'm wondering.

Well, I'm not going to let you get ahead of yourself. But we can go back to WMR, where Hyde started in the French Quarter, and Hyde elevated itself to go up on Dryad Street in the Louisiana Life Building. Go ahead. I'm sorry.

All right, well. I'm sorry. Let me ask a question. I had a broader question I was going to get back to WMR. Why do you think, finally, at this point in time, that there is black radio, finally? All right.

All right. You've got to remember. Now, we started talking about the black newspapers. The three black newspapers we had, the Informer Sentinel, La Courier, and Louisiana Wheeler, showed pictures of Conk Basie, Duke Ellington, Jimmy Liggins, Billy Eckstein, Joe Lewis. Image factors that blacks could look up to. Sure. But they had never seen these people. They've only rarely heard them. See, you didn't have jukeboxes. You had jukeboxes, but they were just beginning to highlight the black intelligentsia and entertainment. All right. But we wanted to see them, and we wanted to hear more about them. Remember, in the 1940s and the early 50s, white disc jockeys, whenever they picked up a record by Louis Armstrong, a Conk Basie or Duke Ellington, they said race records. They didn't say rock and roll. Rock and roll didn't come along until Elvis Presley started shaking his hips, you see. So that was the difference. But eventually, here's what made it much better for us. In the little areas like down in Plaquemines Parish, like in St. Bernard, like over in Jefferson, the West Bank of the River, in West Regal, moreover, people wanted to see what they were doing, and the other people wanted to see what they looked like. We wanted to be there with them. We wanted to give them support. And the biggest problem was trying to stay away from women. That was a good-looking kid with Indian-type features, cold black curly hair. He looked like a black Indian. He's a very handsome man. Well, myself, I don't want to brag, but I felt to believe that I had a certain type of physical qualities in my early 20s that sort of gave me a certain type of splendor in order to deal with life and with people, to extol my virtues and pass them on to somebody and say that I'm a gentleman of quality. Sure. Well, of course you are. So I did that.
But you met a lot of women, huh, Tex?

Oh, boy. It was a lot of fun. It was a lot of fun. We enjoyed ourselves. Oh, wow. Because you know, you didn't want to go crazy or nothing like that, because they had women everywhere, and they just wanted to take you home to dinner. And some women did, and some women took us out to cocktails at the various clubs. In fact, I hardly had to spend any money because, you know, then you had companies and advertisers who felt proud to, like the Falstead Brewing Company and the Blatt's Brewing Company and the Jack's Brewing Company. They all wanted to do something for us, you know. They wanted to come down to the club and invite the people, or come down to the plant and let the people see how we operate. There's so much that happened from 1950 until 1962 until I just couldn't put it, you wouldn't have enough tapes for me to put it on. It's just something that went on.

Well, let's see what we can do. But my point was, why is this all coming, why are blacks becoming, why is it becoming relevant now? I mean, in 1950, and that wasn't happening in 1940 or 1930. Why at that time period?

Well, at that time you were beginning to see a change in the political structure of the state and of the nation. Remember, you had, like I said earlier, you had the White Citizen Council. Then you had the Ku Klux Klan with threats. In 1955, 54, 55, here comes Martin Luther King. All right, so he made a lot of white people mad. But you've got to remember, in 1955, April 24, 1955, Emmett Till went to Sumner, Mississippi, came from Chicago, and so they claimed he winked at a white woman. He was only 14 years of age, just a young boy. Well, the situation in Chicago was a little different than it was in New Orleans or anywhere doing the South. But you know what they did? They took Emmett Till out one night, and they lynched him. That was in 1955. And remember, the black person in here, we've got Ebony Magazine now. Then we've got Our World Magazine. Then we've got the Pittsburgh Courier. We've got the Louisiana Weekly. We've got the Informer Sentinel. Then you've got the Times-Picayune. Then at that time you had the New Orleans Station. You had the New Orleans Item. You had three white papers at the time, too. And they were highlighting what Dr. King was doing, and the Emmett Till story eventually became headlines on white newspapers, and black newspapers just picked it up and started running with it. Then remember, you've got an introduction now of blacks on radio along with whites. Then you've got television slowly beginning to physically show you late evening news what was going on. So remember, blacks were slowly coming together, and the white man hadn't introduced us to crack and to cocaine. All we had was a few weeds, you know, marijuanas, or either, as we would say, to get to, let me have a roach or something like that. They called it a roach, you know, or a weed or something. But you didn't have the killing as I go back in life to read old newspapers and look at my files. Blacks only had a few knives and a few razors. Occasionally some of the guys from off Rampart Street in and around Rampart. Those who had to build their dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
Okay, reel number three with Tech Stevens, August 29, 1995. Okay. Yeah, well you...
Well, I'm not going to let it bother me, believe you me.
Well, uh, real...
By the way, Ted, give me that material other than the newspaper over there. See, all this stuff is for me, too. I don't know where you saw it.
Yeah. You saw...
Yeah, I've seen most of that.
Okay, real number four with Tex Stevens, and this is still August 29th, 1995. Okay, uh, yeah, uh, where were we? Were we talking about Frank Panae? We were moving along. Well in 19...

...his... Right after the soldiers started coming home, and then some soldiers were passing through, and like we said, things were not as integrated as they are now, and people wanted to... People had a few money. Some people were covered being, uh, turned loose and normal with three, four, five, six hundred dollars, which was a lot of money. Remember, Coca-Cola was 25 cents, uh, Coca-Cola was five cents a bottle. You could get a half a pint of liquor for 45 cents, along with a seven-up of Coke and a pitcher of water. Uh, you lived good. And if you spent a dollar, boy, you were really big time in the place, because you got two half pints, or either you got your pint of liquor for about 95 cents or whatever. But here is the dew drop. Here was Frank Panae exploring new horizons, places where he had never been before, but he was trying, because why? He wanted to make sure that his club, in the name of the dew drop, which was two little words, but it became nationwide. Why? Because you're in a major city. Everything is segregated. You got your radio stations blasting the dew drop every day on the air. You got Ray Charles coming in. You got Big Joe Turner coming in. You got Nat King Cole coming in. You got James Brown coming in. You got the Blazers coming in. You got so many different acts and so many different names. Little Miss Cornshuck's one of my favorite people. Anytime she was there, I was always there. She was funny, but she could sing. So all in all, the dew drop imported more out of town name talent between 1945 and 1960 than any other person in town, other than the promoters like Jackson, Rip Roberts, or maybe some of the other promoters like Larry McKinley and a few others. Now, Larry McKinley promoted more big time acts, continuous, than any other promoter that we have until all of a sudden the entertainers themselves, they wanted a special limousine for themselves, a special limousine for their lady friend, or then they wanted fruit, a fruit bowl behind stage with concession of all kinds of sandwiches, and they wanted high powered liquors and wines for a special party for their traveling group. So Larry said he had to get out of that sometimes, you know, beside paying the taxes that the city wanted for the auditorium or city park. He would have to come up with an extra five or ten thousand dollars almost for these two limousines and also for this fruit salad, for this food, and for all this extra liquor. And then they got some guys who probably never drank the most expensive brands, but when they're on the road with Al Green or if they're on the road with Big Joe Turner, they want to be seen drinking the best of everything and eating the best of everything and throwing the best of everything away. That's what's saying. So Larry said we got to get away from that. But Frank Pena, like I said, the only competition that he had at that particular time was probably the Robin Hood with Bennett Ross who on a day to day basis were, well they were just about a half a mile apart, but they were the very best of friends. Sometimes they would swap talent. Sometimes Paul Gaten would probably leave the Robin Hood and go play Frank Pena, but his mainstay was strictly with the Robin Hood. That's where I first saw him, he and Annie Laurie. And Paul Gaten was a tremendous talent. And like I said, Frank Pena knew how to put things together. He knew how to spend money. And he had an advantage by having a hotel in the back with about 20 to 30 rooms. See, he could take care of a band, take care of the entertainer, and they didn't have to worry about going downtown because they couldn't go downtown anyway because everything was segregated. And so Frank had the advantage over most clubs because he had the facility for the entertainment. He had the facility for people to relax themselves. He had the facility for people to relax themselves. He had the restaurant and the lounge there. What else more did you want? Because you had it all for his hand right in front of you right then and there. And so Frank had the advantage over most clubs, because he had the facility for the entertainment, he had the facility for people to relax themselves, he had the restaurant and the lounge there, what else more did you want? Because you had it all for his hand right in front of you, right then and there.
He had the whole package. He had the package.
He had the package.
What about some of the, I was talking about the ancillary clubs, and like, you know, like Foster's? How was Foster's?

George Foster was two blocks from the Doudrop, still right there on LaSalle Street. George Foster had the little downtown club, I mean the uptown club, and he wasn't the promoter that Frank Pena was. He was the guy who fell in line. But he started bringing in, like, well he had brought in Roy Brown, then he had a combination with Roy Brown, and went on the Irish with the first Battle of the Blues that I could recall in the city of New Orleans. That went on for around about maybe five hours between the two of them. And then Amos Milburn left the Dewdrop and came down to Foster's Club and Hotel, and they battled there for a while. It was a lot of fun. I'll never forget because that particular night I think Okie Doke and myself, we all went, we were just hanging out, disc jockeys hanging out together just having a good time. And I think that, let me see who else was in town at that particular time. Well, I think, well the Dewdrop had its show going with Bob Parker and Patsy Vidalia down there. And I'm trying to think of the guy from out of town who was a blues singer, and I love to listen to him. I'm trying to think of his name, it's on the tip of my tongue right now. I'm trying to think about this guy. It just doesn't come to me right now. But he was, he, tremendous blues. Billy Wright is his name. Oh, Billy Wright, from Atlanta. From Atlanta. Yeah. Blues for my baby. Right. He could let him, he could. What was his big song? Blues for my baby and You Satisfied. That was a too big, that's too big a song. Then he had.
Straight A, not straight A's. Something about Aces.
Yeah, the Aces for this. You know I'd like to get a copy of that. You know anybody who would have it?
I had a Billy Wright, I had some Billy Wright records.
I'd like to know who has it, I'd like to get a copy of that.

I don't have any Billy Wright records. I had a Billy Wright record. I have. You know my collection's in the back, and somehow, you know the years. I can understand that. Right. Something just disappears in that black hole. Right, right, right. My Billy Wright record just disappeared. Not from the archive, but before, some reason before the archive.
Well I'm glad the archives is here because we can bring them here and protect them.
Oh yeah, well that's why they're here.
I got some more stuff I gotta bring up here.
Oh, I hope so. So yeah, so Frank, so Foster's really wasn't as much competition.

No, but it had an advantage though, because you see, here's what, because when you were not at the Dew Drop you could walk two blocks down and go to Foster and see something like the French Quarter with clubs right next door to one another. So you got a guy who can walk from one area to another and you know, you say, well, you know you get tired of sitting in the same place. You got your lady friend, let's go to another venue and get a drink and let's do our thing and let's get it together. So that's, you know.
Could you walk to Robin Hood? Oh yeah.
Yeah, because the Robin Hood was only what, four or five blocks away. Right, it was right down there on the corner of Jackson Avenue.
So that area you could say, people would, club hop.
Right, club hop. You wouldn't need an automobile. But today's a different one.
But now there wasn't any, now, did the Dew Drop have a cover to get in?

No. Sometimes yes, it all depends. If he had that out of town talent, he would probably be like, let's say dollar and ten cents, dollar twenty-five cents maybe. Rarely did Frank have anything over two dollars at that time because two dollars was a lot of money. Yeah. But everything was a dollar, dollar and a half, or seventy-five cents or whatever. You know.
Rarely. Was it the same for the Fosters and for Robin Hood?

Just about, because you know you had similar talents. And it wasn't no more than about twenty-five to fifty cents difference one place or the other. Because I can remember Louis Armstrong coming to New Orleans here, playing something for fifty cents or seventy-five cents. I had it here someplace. I was just trying to wonder what I'd do with it.
Was that the, why don't you tell me about Louis now that we got Johnny? When's the first time you saw him in New Orleans? You saw Louis in New Orleans?
First time I saw Louis in New Orleans was 1935.
You saw him in thirty- you saw him in thirty-five.

In 1935 I saw him. Where was that? I tell you he was over in Algiers. I think he went over there to talk to some friends or somebody. And it so happened that I was on, I was on Test Street and Louis Armstrong was in the automobile with somebody. And it just so happened that he stopped. And I said, wow, boy, Louis Armstrong. Boy, I felt good because I had heard his music and I had seen his picture in the paper. And I went over to shake hands but I couldn't shake hands with him because the car was moving so fast. And you know I'm a small person, 1935. And I said, boy, one of these good days I'd like to get the clue to Louis Armstrong. Boy, so here comes 1949 and here I am, an escort driving his car, make sure that he gets on his float and this, that, and the other so forth and so on. Wherever he and his wife went I was right there with them.
How'd you get to be Louis' escort?

I don't know, it just, I tell you what happened. By being in radio and working for a newspaper, here I'm a press man. And everybody in the Zulu Club at that time, they knew me. Especially Ernest Wright who thought the world of me. I was a big name person in New Orleans because he was affiliated with a lot of unions and with churches and so forth and so on. So between Ernest Wright and Jim Russell and Jim Poole who was a big wheel in the Zulus at that particular time. God bless him. So that's how I got to become one of the escorts for Louis Armstrong. To drive the automobile to take him where he wanted to go and this, that, and the other so forth and so on. And the second time that I, and then as you, the program, when he played at Booker T, wherever he played at Collison Arena. There I was right there emceeing these shows. I emceed for two or three times that Louis Armstrong came to New Orleans. I emceed these shows. So I felt pretty good knowing Satchmo. I was proud to know him. And to say that he was from New Orleans. He was a premier individual in my mind because he had the talent. He looked the part and knowing that he had come from down below the general average. A man who could not sleep in a downtown hotel, but yet he was highlighted all over the world, but in the town where he was born, they turned his back. It's just like the program that Al Corbetti sent me when they put this big building up in honor of Louis Armstrong, they still haven't finished the next Louis Armstrong Memorial Project. It's something that he was working on way back in 1973. That's the letter there. But then again, like I was saying just a little while ago, there was Louis Armstrong playing at the U.S. Army Base on Poland and Dauphin, August 29, 1931. Now let's see, what was the price on that? Is there a price there? I can't even see the price. No, I'm not seeing a... But it was what, 35 to 50 cents back in 31?
Yeah, that was, yeah. That's about all it would have been.

Because you got to remember the banks had closed in 1929. Hardly anybody had any money in 30 and 31. And that's when you had tokens on the market. You don't remember the little tokens. No, I'm not. If you spent 15 cents or 25 cents, you had to come up with a token. Then they had this thing about half red beans and half rice, or either one-third meat, one-third beans, and one-third rice. So if you spent 50 cents, you could go home and cook yourself a dinner with half red beans, or one-third red beans, rice, and meat. You know, we have come through something in this state and in this country. This is really wild.
This is a...where's this from? I'm looking at this. That's out the Louisiana Weekly.
It's out the Weekly, okay. Out the Weekly, August 29, 1931.
This is of Louis Armstrong playing at... At Poland. He's playing for a hospital benefit. A benefit. A hospital work for colored at the U.S. Army Supply Base. Right. Which is at Poland and Dolphin.
Oh, Poland. And it's still there.
Is it still there?

It is. It's still there. It is. Okay. It's still there. In fact, I spoke there for Black History Week, round about, I think about maybe about six years ago. And then, last year, I went with my wife and several other friends. They had a big Mardi Gras fair, promoted by one of the outstanding lady clubs here in the city of New Orleans. So, they still got things going on down in Poland and Dauphine. It's not just an army base. They have enough facility and space where you can go there and have a party or enjoy yourself and have a good time. And I only wish getting back to Frank Pena. I wish he was still alive today because he became one of my very, very dear friends. And he would always call me to help write some of his newspaper continuity. When he didn't feel like putting it together, I wrote some of the copy for him to put it in the Louisiana Weekly, Pittsburgh Courier, or even in the Informer Sentinel. And then, when it came to putting it on the radio, I wrote whatever was on my program, I wrote the continuity for it for Frank Pena. And that's what he liked about me. I tell you, in fact, Frank Pena liked me so much until Christmas 1953. He called me. He said, Tex, come up, I want to see you. When I hit the door, Frank had a brand new suit hanging there waiting for me. First time other than myself buying my own suit, somebody gave me a suit for a present. That was Frank Pena, and I'll forget that.
Did he treat a lot of people like that? Was he very generous?

Well, he was generous to a lot of people. Frank was a likable individual who just cared for people, and he just liked to get involved. And I was thinking about, I had a meeting with Frank Pena and Rosenthal from out of Port Arthur, Texas. I'm trying to think of Rosenthal. He had a theater and a nightclub, and he used to come here and talk to Frank Pena all the time. Sometimes Frank would send some of his talent over there to Orange, Texas, rather. Charlie Rosenthal was his name. Very nice man. I hope he's still alive. He was a guy who, he and Frank Pena were the very best of friends, and they took a liking to each other, and they would swap talent from time to time. People would, Earl King would probably leave the Dew Drop and go over to the Orange, Texas, and play either Smile or Lewis. Otherwise, they helped to keep the black experience, entertainment experience alive. And I like that. But today it's a different kind of ball game because most of those clubs, the, the, uh, Blue Drop is not what it used to be. It's a shadow of its former self. There's no more live entertainment there, I think. Uh, um, they had live entertainment there sometimes. Last year, just a temporary thing. Uh, but it was not the glory days of yesteryear with the big name talent that, uh, Frank Pena used to promote. Uh, the club is kind of run down. There's no place to park. Yeah. Like you could do in the forties and early forties and fifties. Everybody has an automobile nowadays. More people are living in the project now. And then you have a lot of broken down cars parked in the neighborhood. Uh, then, uh, your dope addicts, uh, uh, are now promenading all over the neighborhood now. And it's kind of dangerous out there. Uh, uh, you don't want to be caught in that neighborhood when it's getting dark. Yeah. It's, it, it, it's sad to say. But you will never see the dew drop of yesteryear again, like when it was in its glory, when Frank Pena was living. You will never see that. But you will always have the name of the dew drop whenever anybody get ready to write the history of jazz, blues, and big name entertainment of the South. And Frank Pena and the dew drop has to be mentioned in these articles, no doubt about it.

Oh, definitely. One point. Earl King told me, he said one of the, the most successful, the recent success of the dew drop wasn't, and the attraction wasn't just the music. He said, but he said a lot, the transvestites and the gay reviews.
Well, you had, well, you had Patsy Vidalia who was, uh, you know, a gay person. Right. But Patsy had the personality to bring people like Billy Wright who was, from what I understand.
Billy was gay, we can say.
And they had a couple others. And, uh, you had, uh, Matty Campbell who was a gay person. And then you had, uh, fancy fucking Fanny, oh. It's okay, it's okay.
It's alright. Oh my goodness.
Look what I've said on the microphone.
No, that's okay.
Hey man, you better cut that, you better cut that out.
No, we're okay.

Don't worry. That was Fanny Dixon who, uh, came from out front of town. I never knew anything about her people, but, uh, she was a big time named type of prostitute, who used to work the streets. Now, I think she had a pimp once or twice, but somehow or another she got rid of the pimp, and she started working for herself. Uh, but all in all, like I said, those days are gone. Uh, and the houses of prostitution that we had up and down Rampart Street, up and down Dryad Street, and what we had uptown, uh, when, uh, when big time Kutchin, whispering boots, and Axe Handle Sam, and all those guys were living. It's all gone. It's, it, it, it's belonged to history now. Uh, a lot of these people left town. Like I said, uh, some time back, the world's greatest pimps came out of the city of New Orleans for a while. But when they started traveling with their women on the road to the various, uh, levee camps, and the country towns with the sugar workers, and start getting into Texas, they taught the fellas in Houston, Texas how to pimp and to go big time. The blacks from Houston, Texas learned from the black pimp cadre in the city of New Orleans and went to New York, and the blacks from Houston, Texas went to New York and took over the pimping business in New York. Today, the big time pimps laid the groundwork for the modern day pimps in New York today, came out of Houston, Texas. And they were like, like Big Al Charleston, Money Man Wilson, uh, Sweet Thing, I'm trying to think of something, what other Sweet Thing name, Sweet Thing Dixon, and these guys were big name guys who made a lot of money. And, uh, it, it all reminded me of a story about Iceberg Slim, who probably was the world's greatest pimp of all time, who, uh, from what I understand, you know, well I know he wrote two books. Uh, I think I, I had the last interview with him about fifteen years ago before he died. Uh, Iceberg Slim was some kind of character. I had a chance to talk to him, the way he talked about women. He could low rate a woman with a culture type of presentation where you know right then and there it's low down when he's talking, but the way he expressed it, he made it feel like it was a part of living culture. I can't, that's the best way I can talk about that. Iceberg Slim, who was a very handsome man who had a full head of beautiful black and gray hair, who was very thin but muscular, who wore his clothes like he walked out of Esquire or Q Magazine or something of that nature. But women just loved him the way he handled himself, uh, you know, by having high powered lawyers, having quality hotels, having doctors to take care of the prostitutes and the hoars.
